claims.text: Cast Co30Cr25Fe25Ni20 has grains larger than 100 μm, limited ductility, and possible segregation.
Severe plastic deformation followed by annealing at 400–500 °C with 0.2–0.4 at.% C can produce a sub-50 nm FCC+HCP Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloy without brittle phases.
Interstitial carbon stabilizes the FCC matrix in a Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-based alloy.
Carbon promotes a metastable, strain-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation in the proposed Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloy.
Carbon segregation reduces grain-boundary energy and suppresses grain growth.
Cryogenic rolling to 90% reduction or high-pressure torsion will refine the proposed alloy to grains smaller than 50 nm.
Annealing at approximately 450 °C for one hour will stabilize the nanocrystalline structure and promote FCC-to-HCP transformation without coarsening.
Joint TWIP and TRIP activity in an FCC+HCP alloy can enhance strength while retaining ductility.
Adding Nb to CoCrFeNi can produce a hard, brittle Co2Nb-type Laves phase.
High Mo additions cause brittle intermetallic formation in Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys.
The processed alloy will contain approximately 30–40 vol.% HCP phase in an FCC matrix.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength greater than 800 MPa.
The processed alloy will have tensile elongation greater than 50%.
Processing will increase hardness by more than 200 HV relative to the cast state.
The cast Co-Cr-Fe-Ni baseline has a yield strength of approximately 300–400 MPa.
The cast Co-Cr-Fe-Ni baseline has less than 10% elongation because of limited work hardening and casting defects.
Annealing above 600 °C causes grain growth and loss of the HCP phase.
Carbon contents above 0.6 at.% create a risk of brittle M23C6 carbide formation.
Increasing Ni raises stacking-fault energy enough to suppress HCP formation.
An FCC+HCP dual-phase structure prevents brittle intermetallic formation.

contradictions.description: The target grain size is below 50 nm, but the hypothesis is only declared falsified when grain size exceeds 100 nm; a result between 50 and 100 nm would fail the stated prediction without meeting the falsification rule.

Detection of carbides or brittle phases is stated to falsify the hypothesis without limiting that rule to the target sample, while brittle behavior in the 0.8 at.% C comparison sample is separately said to support the hypothesis.
